nameStory: The name 'floating-leaved pondweed' perfectly captures this plant's signature look - its broad, oval leaves that float like lily pads on the water's surface. Unlike water lilies though, these leaves are attached to long, flexible stems that anchor deep underwater, allowing them to bob and drift with gentle currents.
description: Floating-leaved pondweed is an aquatic plant that lives entirely in quiet freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow streams throughout New England. It produces two very different types of leaves: thin, ribbon-like underwater leaves and broader, oval floating leaves that rest on the surface like small lily pads. The plant can grow several feet long, with flexible stems that sway underwater and surface leaves typically 2-4 inches long that create distinctive patches on calm water.

idTips.label: Floating Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to egg-shaped leaves that float flat on the water surface, feeling thick and leathery with prominent parallel veins running from base to tip - unlike the radiating veins of true water lily pads

idTips.label: Underwater Leaves
idTips.description: Thin, ribbon-like submerged leaves that feel delicate and translucent, completely different from the floating leaves on the same plant

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, dense spikes of tiny greenish flowers that stick up above the water surface on thick stalks, feeling firm and cylindrical to the touch

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Long, flexible underwater stems that feel smooth and rubbery, easily bending without breaking as they connect the floating leaves to roots in the mud below

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies of floating leaves connected by underwater stems, creating patches that look like scattered green plates on the water surface

habitat: Look for floating-leaved pondweed in quiet freshwater environments like ponds, shallow lake bays, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It prefers water 1-6 feet deep with muddy or sandy bottoms where its roots can anchor securely. You'll often find it growing alongside other aquatic plants like water lilies, cattails, and pickerelweed in nutrient-rich waters.

seasonality.spring: New floating leaves emerge and unfurl on the surface as water temperatures warm, starting small and gradually expanding. Underwater ribbon leaves are also growing but harder to spot from shore.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full-sized floating leaves creating obvious patches on the water surface. Flower spikes appear above water in mid to late summer, looking like small green bottlebrushes.
seasonality.fall: Floating leaves may turn yellowish and begin to decay, while flowers develop into small, hard fruits. Some leaves persist until first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: All above-water parts die back and sink, leaving only roots and underground stems alive in the mud to regrow next spring.

funFact: This plant is like an underwater transformer - it produces completely different types of leaves depending on whether they'll live above or below water, with the same plant making both delicate underwater ribbons and tough floating pads perfectly suited to their different environments!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small water lily pads, but pondweed leaves have parallel veins running from base to tip (like grass) while water lily leaves have veins radiating out from where the stem attaches (like spokes on a wheel). Remember: parallel = pondweed, radiating = lily.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Potamogeton literally means 'river neighbor' in Greek, though this species actually prefers still waters over flowing rivers. There are over 20 different pondweed species in New England, making this one of our most diverse aquatic plant groups.
compareHints: Among New England's many pondweeds, floating-leaved pondweed is unique in having large, obvious floating leaves - most other pondweeds have only thin underwater leaves or much smaller floating leaves. Broad-leaved pondweed has similar floating leaves but they're typically larger and more heart-shaped, while ribbon-leaved pondweed has much narrower floating leaves that look more like straps than ovals.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many pondweeds, ribbon-leaved pondweed stands out for its distinctly long, narrow leaves that are much more ribbon-like than grass-like.
Among New England's many pondweeds, broad-leaved pondweed is distinguished by having some of the widest underwater leaves with the most veins.

Unlike floating-leaved pondweed which has oval leaves that float on the surface, or ribbon-leaved pondweed with its narrow straight leaves, curly-leaf pondweed's leaves stay completely underwater and have those unmistakable wavy, crimped edges.
Unlike ribbon-leaved and floating-leaved pondweeds which produce leaves that reach the water surface, Robbins' pondweed stays completely submerged throughout its life cycle.
Unlike floating-leaved pondweed which has leaves that float on the surface, perfoliate pondweed stays completely submerged.
Among New England's many pondweed species, longleaf pondweed stands out for having both underwater and floating leaves on long stalks - most relatives specialize in just one leaf type.

Among the pondweeds, Richardson's stands out for its relatively broad, crinkly-edged underwater leaves - much wider than grass-leaved or ribbon-leaved pondweed, but not as broad as the truly wide-leaved species like broad-leaved pondweed.
Among the many pondweed species in New England, spiral pondweed is unique for its twisted flower spikes – no other pondweed has this corkscrew feature.
Among New England's many pondweed species, grass-leaved pondweed stands out for its consistently narrow, grass-like submerged leaves that vary in length on the same plant.
Among the many New England pondweeds, eel-grass pondweed stands out for its extremely narrow, ribbon-like leaves that never float on the surface.
Among New England's many pondweeds, snailseed pondweed is most similar to other narrow-leaved species like Berchtold's and small pondweed, sharing the thin, linear leaves and small stature.

Berchtold's pondweed stands out from other New England pondweeds by having the narrowest leaves in the genus - much thinner than the ribbon-like leaves of ribbon-leaved pondweed or the broader blades of floating-leaved pondweed.
Among the many pondweed species in New England, white-stemmed pondweed is distinguished by its pale stems and preference for deeper, clearer water.

Among New England's pondweeds, Oakes' stands out for its extremely narrow, delicate leaves that are much thinner than the ribbon-like leaves of grass-leaved pondweed or the broader leaves of floating-leaved species.
Among New England's many pondweed species, spotted pondweed is the only one with translucent windows in its leaves.

Among New England's many pondweeds, leafy pondweed stands out for its extremely thin, hair-like leaves - much finer than broad-leaved pondweed's oval leaves or curly-leaf pondweed's wavy, serrated foliage.
Among New England's many pondweeds, Bluntleaf Pondweed stands out for its consistently blunt leaf tips, while most others like Ribbon-leaved Pondweed have pointed tips.
Among its many pondweed relatives, small pondweed stands out for having the most thread-like, delicate leaves - much thinner than grass-leaved pondweed or spiral pondweed.
Among New England's many pondweeds, northern pondweed stands out with its reddish stem coloration - most other species like ribbon-leaved pondweed or grass-leaved pondweed have plain green stems.
Among the many pondweed species in New England, Hill's pondweed stands out for its strict requirement for alkaline water and its rarity.

Among all the pondweeds, this species stands out for having by far the thinnest leaves – other pondweeds have ribbon-like, oval, or broader linear leaves, but none approach the hair-fine texture of Algae-like Pondweed.
Among New England's many pondweed species, shining pondweed stands out for its consistently glossy leaves - most other pondweeds have matte or only slightly shiny foliage.
Among the thin-leaved pondweeds, Vasey's pondweed is distinguished by very specific technical features of its fruits and stipules (small leaf-like structures at the leaf base).

Among New England's many pondweed species, Straightleaf Pondweed stands out for its rigid, upright leaf posture - most other pondweeds have either floating leaves, wavy underwater leaves, or much more flexible foliage.
